Empirical Research Plan: “How Valuable Are Suharto Connections to Indonesian Firms?”

====================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Multi-event, difference-in-differences event study (sometimes called “cross-sectional event study”).

Rationale
• Multiple discrete, well-dated information shocks (6 Suharto-health rumors) allow us to treat each as a short-horizon “experiment.”  
• Very short windows (1–3 trading days) mean fundamentals cannot change; price moves reflect revised expectations about political rents.  
• The Castle “Suharto-dependence” index gives ex-ante cross-sectional variation in treatment intensity.  
• Combining the time dimension (before vs. after each rumor) with the cross-section (high vs. low dependence) delivers a DID design for each event; stacking events yields additional power.  

Why not IV/RDD?
• No obvious instrument and no running variable with cutoff.  
• The causal variation is sharp and discrete, making a standard event-study/DID hybrid the cleanest approach.


====================================================================
2. Treatment and Control Definition
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated_i = 1 if firm i has a Suharto-dependence score ≥ 4 (top two quintiles); 0 otherwise.  
(Alternative: use the 1–5 score continuously; results should be monotonic.)

Control group  
Firms with scores ≤ 2 (lowest two quintiles). Mid-range (=3) can be either dropped or used as an intermediate group in robustness tests.

Timing / event date  
Six rumor dates supplied in the news chronology. For each event e, define:  
• Day 0 = first trading day the rumor appears in Indonesian media.  
• Window = [-1, +1] trading days (main), [-3, +3] (robustness).  
Negative-health rumors are “bad” news; positive-health denials are “good” news.  

Outcome  
Cumulative abnormal return (CAR) over the chosen window.

No running variable → RDD not applicable.


====================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Exogeneity of health news: Rumors about Suharto’s health are plausibly unrelated to contemporaneous firm-specific shocks.  
Plausibility: High—health shocks are biological and largely orthogonal to daily corporate news.

A2. No systematic information leakage differentially by dependence group before Day -1.  
Plausibility: Reasonable but testable—check for pre-trend in returns (event-time ‑10 to ‑2).

A3. Market efficiency/semi-strong form: Prices impound all publicly available information immediately.  
Plausibility: Jakarta market was liquid for large firms; 1–3-day windows are standard.

A4. Parallel trends in normal times: In the absence of Suharto-health news, high- and low-dependence firms would have similar average returns.  
Plausibility: Needs to be shown—verify with long pre-event window.

A5. No other confounding macro news that coincides with the six rumor dates.  
Plausibility: Must be checked—consult news wires, include market index in CAR estimation, drop events contaminated by, e.g., big IMF announcements.


====================================================================
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Confounding macro/political news on the same day (e.g. exchange-rate moves).  
Mitigation:  
• Read same-day newspapers/wires; flag “dirty” events.  
• Re-estimate excluding contaminated events; results should be similar.  

Threat 2: Anticipation or leakage that starts several days before the rumor.  
Mitigation:  
• Plot average abnormal returns from ‑10 to ‑2; require they be statistically zero.  
• Narrow the window if leakage is detected or adjust event date back by one trading day.

Threat 3: Measurement error in the Castle dependence score (subjective ratings).  
Mitigation:  
• Show robustness to alternative codings (continuous score, terciles, top-10 vs. others).  
• Instrument the Castle score with objective proxies (e.g., board membership of Suharto family) in a 2SLS robustness exercise.


====================================================================
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Required packages
library(data.table)      # Fast data wrangling
library(fixest)          # High-performance panel/DID regressions
library(quantmod)        # Market model estimation (optional)
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------------
returns   <- fread("jse_daily_returns_95_97.csv")        # firm_id, date, ret
depend    <- fread("suharto_dependence.csv")             # firm_id, score (1–5)
events    <- fread("health_rumor_events.csv")            # event_id, date, type(+/-)
market_xt <- fread("jse_composite_returns.csv")          # date, mkt_ret

# 2. Merge & variable construction ---------------------------------
df <- merge(returns, depend, by = "firm_id")
df <- merge(df, market_xt, by = "date")

# Market-model residuals (abnormal returns)
# Estimate α_i, β_i on pre-event period 1994-01-01 to 1995-12-31
pre <- df[date < as.Date("1996-01-01")]
alpha_beta <- pre[, {
  fit <- lm(ret ~ mkt_ret)
  list(alpha = coef(fit)[1], beta = coef(fit)[2])
}, by = firm_id]

df <- merge(df, alpha_beta, by = "firm_id")
df[, abret := ret - alpha - beta * mkt_ret]

# 3. Build event-time panel ----------------------------------------
event_window <- function(event_day, w = 1) {
  seq(event_day - w, event_day + w, by = 1)
}

# Expand events to window
ev_dt <- events[, .(date = event_window(as.Date(date), w = 1)), 
                by = .(event_id, type)]

df <- merge(df, ev_dt, by = "date", allow.cartesian = TRUE)
df[, car := sum(abret), by = .(firm_id, event_id)]   # CAR[-1,+1]

# Keep unique firm-event observations
car_df <- unique(df[, .(firm_id, event_id, car, type, score)])

# Treatment dummy and controls
car_df[, treated := as.integer(score >= 4)]
car_df <- merge(car_df, depend[, .(firm_id, size, gov_own, industry)], by = "firm_id")

# 4. Main DID regression -------------------------------------------
# type = -1 for negative health news, +1 for positive (optional interaction)
est <- feols(car ~ treated * type + size + gov_own + i(industry),
             data = car_df, cluster = "firm_id")
summary(est)

# 5. Robustness check: placebo (random dates) ----------------------
set.seed(123)
placebo <- copy(events)
placebo[, date := sample(unique(returns$date), .N)]  # randomize
# (Repeat steps to compute placebo CARs and re-estimate; coefficient should be ~0)
```

====================================================================
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Direction: For negative-health rumors (higher perceived likelihood Suharto will exit), CARs for high-dependence firms should be significantly negative relative to low-dependence firms. For positive rumors the sign flips.  
• Magnitude: Prior studies of political-connection value in emerging markets suggest losses of ‑2 % to ‑6 % on one-day windows for strongly connected firms. Given the 1990s Indonesian volatility, a ‑4 % CAR differential (high vs. low) over a [-1,+1] window is plausible.

====================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Event-Study/DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Clearly identified, well-dated shocks       1  
C2: No confounding events on same days       0 (must be verified)  
C3: No differential pre-trends/leakage        1 (testable)  
C4: Parallel trends in normal times           1 (checked)  
C5: Stable treatment classification over time    1 (Castle score is time-invariant for 95-97)  

Total = 4 / 5 → overall design appears credible but hinges on cleaning contaminated events.
